<STATEMENT>
# Problem C — Proof of Impossibility

Time limit: 2 s   Memory limit: 256 MB

The factory still has only two shifts, 1 and 2, but the roster is known to be
hopeless. Your job is not to assign shifts — it is to certify the impossibility. It is
guaranteed that there is at least one set of three workers such that every worker in the set cannot share a shift with any other worker in the set. Any such group proves two shifts cannot suffice. Output one such set.

## Input
The first line contains two integers n and m (3 ≤ n ≤ 2000,
3 ≤ m ≤ min(n·(n−1)/2, 2·10⁵)).
Each of the next m lines contains two integers u v, indicating that worker u and worker v cannot be assigned to the same shift.
It is guaranteed that at least one such group of three workers exists.

## Output
Print three integers a b c on one line with a < b < c such that worker a cannot share a shift with worker b, worker a cannot share with c, and worker b cannot share with c. Output the lexicographically smallest such group (smallest a; ties by smallest b; then smallest c).

## Example 1
Input:
```
4 5
1 2
1 3
2 3
2 4
3 4
```
Output:
```
1 2 3
```

## Example 2
Input:
```
5 6
1 2
1 4
2 4
3 4
3 5
4 5
```
Output:
```
1 2 4
```
</STATEMENT>

The model must now map these localized interaction rules back to the structural requirement of finding a 3-clique (triangle) in the implied graph.
</RATIONALE>

The requested output is still exactly the lexicographically smallest set of three mutually incompatible elements.
</PRESERVED_ANSWER>

The problem remains exactly the task of finding a triangle in an unweighted undirected graph, which has the same time complexity and algorithmic requirements.
</PRESERVED_CLASS>
